notes.short: Stones and rafters cry out against the builder
notes.about: The stones of the wall cry out and the rafters echo them, as if the house could speak. The picture shows that every part of a house built by unjust gain (verse 9) bears witness against the man who built it. Some add that it cries out to God for vengeance.

figure.name: Personification
figure.words: the stones will cry out from the wall, and the rafters will echo it from the woodwork
figure.means: the house built by plunder and cruelty bearing witness against its builder and, some add, crying to God for vengeance

notes.evidence: Calvin calls it a new personification: the prophet gives speech to stone and wood, and every part of the building cries that it was built by plunder. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) also calls it personification: the stones testify against the plunderer. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes): such works have a voice that cries to God. Clarke: stone and timber are represented as calling for vengeance.

cites.quote: There is here introduced by the Prophet a new personification. … He now ascribes speech to stones and wood, of which buildings are formed. … there is no part of the building that will not cry out that it was built by plunder, by cruelty, and, in a word, by evil deeds.
personification. The very stones of thy palace built by rapine shall testify against thee

notes.short: A saying the plundered nations will take up
notes.about: The nations the conqueror gathered to himself (verse 5) will turn his deeds into a saying against him: “Woe to him who amasses what is not his.” Short and pointed, it would be repeated everywhere when the plunderer fell.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: Woe to him who amasses what is not his
figure.means: the saying the wronged nations will repeat against the plunderer: wealth taken from others brings him woe, not gain

original.note: In Hebrew “taunt” is mashal, a word for a short, pointed saying.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Parœmia, among proverbs first found in Scripture. Calvin says this woe would be said everywhere, the mashal being a short, pithy saying worth remembering. Henry says those triumphing in the tyrant's fall are given a taunting proverb, the woe its words. E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) has the nations sing a dirge of woes: proverbs saying much in few words.
notes.limit: The verse foretells a saying the nations will take up when he falls; it does not say the words were already in use. It is the first of five woes in the chapter (verses 6, 9, 12, 15 and 19).

cites.at: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture, p. 763
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture; but, which, owing to their fulness of meaning and their wide application, have since passed into general use as proverbial sayings ... “Shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb against him, and say, ‘Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his!
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: all these would at length take up against them parables and taunts; and what would be said everywhere would be this ... Woe to him who increases and enriches himself by things not his own. ... meshil is a short saying or a pithy sentence, and worthy to be remembered

Those that shall triumph in the fall of this great tyrant are here furnished with a parable, and a taunting proverb, to take up against him. He shall say (he that draws up the insulting ditty shall say thus), Ho, he that increases that which is not his!

As one vast choir in one terrible varied chant of all those thousand thousand voices, to sing a dirge over him of the judgments of God which his ill-doings to them should bring upon him, a fivefold Woe, woe, woe, woe, woe! ... It is the character of these proverbs to say much in few words, sometimes in one, and more than appears.
